item.title: Ep 17 – The control plane wakes up (26 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Today’s episode follows a common shift across the AI stack: frontier systems are becoming less about standalone demos and more about operational loops, from protein design to agent protocols to security control planes.

GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities (OpenAI, 2026-11-24): OpenAI reports GPT‑6 protein-design experiments with wet-lab binding hits, while noting specialized biology models still helped with filtering and selection.

MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude (Anthropic / Claude, 2026-11-24): Anthropic introduces Skills over MCP in public beta, with Tasks and Elicitation generally available in Claude and Claude Code.

99 IPs but a C2 ain’t one: An Active Intrusion Campaign Against Check Point Security Management Servers (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23): GreyNoise details GT13 activity against Check Point Security Management Servers, including 24 affected management servers and suspected AI-assisted activity.

Hackers compromise Check Point Servers in 22 organizations (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-24): Coverage notes the campaign affected at least 22 organizations and says the AI-use claim remains unconfirmed.

Hackers Compromise 24 Check Point Management Servers in Suspected AI-Driven Attack Campaign (The Hacker News, 2026-11-25): Follow-up reporting includes Check Point’s statement that the activity involved a previously disclosed, patched vulnerability and was not a new exploitation technique.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Cloudloop”, “Curiousity”, “Glass Android”, “Bigger Questions”, “Time to Think”, “Under Suspicion”, “Evening Glow” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive / OpenGameArt; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0); “30 CC0 SFX loops” by rubberduck (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: A general-purpose model just designed protein binders that worked in a wet lab.

B: Not perfectly, and not alone. But enough to move AI from demo toward operating system for science.

* * *

A: Hello, I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Thursday the 26th of November, and this is Almost Human 365.

A: Today, the frontier stack gets practical: molecules, agent protocols, and the security systems attackers want to own.

A: OpenAI published research saying GPT-6 can design protein shapes and amino-acid sequences with reasoning and code, without a specialized biology model generating the first draft.

B: Its announcement says the models can design “new protein shapes” and their chemical building blocks “using only reasoning and code.”

A: Specialized biology models still helped with sequences, filtering, and candidate selection before lab testing.

B: With Onava, OpenAI tested 322 GPT-6.2 minibinders against five targets. Thirty-five bound, or 10.9%.

A: Redesign looked stronger: 75 of 88 MDM2 designs bound, 26 of 42 for VEGF-A, and 8 of 59 for PD-1.

B: In antibody work, 128 of 182 VHH designs bound IL-4R alpha.

A: But OpenAI says this still does not prove end-to-end zero-shot de novo minibinder generation without specialized help.

B: And for full structure prediction, its internal model scored 0.38 TM-score, versus 0.93 for ESMFold2.

A: The model did not replace the stack; it earned a seat inside it.

* * *

A: That verified loop connects to Anthropic’s MCP update.

B: Last episode, Claude moved into pull-request review and approvals. Now the protocol layer is becoming more agentic.

A: Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code. Servers can ship instructions, workflows, best practices, or account-specific playbooks alongside tools.

B: Claude loads those skills only when needed, so procedure is available without stuffing every rule into context.

A: Tasks let a server run long operations, even agent loops, while Claude keeps working and collects the result later.

B: Elicitation adds the guardrail: a server can pause a tool call for user input or sign-off before something risky happens.

A: Anthropic’s examples are Supabase confirming costs, Railway asking before destructive service changes, and GitHub requiring a repository name before deletion.

B: The scale is large: more than 700 million monthly SDK downloads, and more than 10,000 connectors for Claude.

A: Developers are packaging when to act, when to wait, and when to ask.

* * *

A: The darker version of that control-plane story is GT13.

B: GreyNoise says the intrusion set compromised 24 Check Point Security Management Servers, affecting at least 22 organizations globally.

A: Confirmed activity ran from October 17 to November 2, across assets in 17 countries and critical sectors.

B: A management server controls firewall policy, certificates, and visibility. Compromise it, and the defender’s map flips.

A: GreyNoise saw 99 IP addresses, more than 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 file events.

B: The actor used a compromised Rejetto HFS server as a relay for command results and stolen data.

A: Post-compromise actions included copying firewall databases and the internal certificate authority, minting pivot dot p twelve, and unloading security policies.

B: That last step would disable the firewall.

A: GreyNoise suspects AI-assisted scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction, though that remains unconfirmed.

B: Check Point said the activity used a previously disclosed, patched vulnerability, not a new technique.

A: GreyNoise’s warning was shorter: “we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing.”

B: The takeaway: reliable control loops help labs and software, but can also make intrusions faster and harder to read.

B: That's Almost Human 365 for today. See you tomorrow.

A: Stay curious, and stay careful.

item.title: Ep 16 – The control plane moves (25 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Today’s episode follows a single shift across software, science, and geopolitics: AI systems are moving into the control plane. Anthropic is putting agents into pull-request review and approval paths, DeepMind is pairing agent search with Lean proofs for quantum algorithms, and U.S. export controls are naming companies tied to advanced-compute diversion risk.

Anthropic launches Claude Ship to help developers ship code faster (Reuters via StreetInsider, 2026-11-23): Claude Ship includes Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals for GitHub pull-request workflows, with PR Steward designed to assist rather than approve or merge code on its own.

Anthropic launches Claude Ship, extending AI-assisted development to pull request approvals (InfoWorld, 2026-11-24): Analysts frame the launch as an evolution of AI-assisted code review into the later review and approval stages of the software development lifecycle.

Anthropic launches Claude Ship to help AI agents review, fix and approve code changes (Mint, 2026-11-24): Coverage highlights Claude Ship’s role in review, repair, and approval workflows for Claude Team and Enterprise users on GitHub.

Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification (Google DeepMind, 2026-11-23): Gemini 4 agent teams found improved quantum algorithms, verified them in Lean, and reported gains including an 11.8x computing-cost reduction for a fusion calculation and a 290x speedup for an arcsin routine.

Additions to the Entity List (U.S. Federal Register / Bureau of Industry and Security, 2026-11-23): BIS added seven entities in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand to the Entity List over advanced computing diversion risk, imposing license requirements with a presumption of denial.

US blacklists Alibaba subsidiary and Megaspeed linked to Nvidia scandal (Reuters via StreetInsider, 2026-11-23): Reuters reported Megaspeed had been under U.S. investigation since 2024 over whether it diverted AI chips to China, and that Alibaba’s Singapore subsidiary Apex was also listed.

Alibaba disputes US blacklisting of S'pore subsidiary over chip rerouting (The Straits Times, 2026-11-24): Alibaba rejected Apex Enterprise Solutions’ Entity List designation as erroneous and said Apex had never diverted restricted advanced computing chips.

inclusionAI/Ling-3.2-air model card (Hugging Face model card): Ant Group’s inclusionAI posted an MIT-licensed, open-weight, native multimodal MoE with 124B total parameters, 5.5B active parameters, and SGLang/vLLM serving notes.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Cloudloop”, “Tech Toys”, “Curiousity”, “Bigger Questions”, “Time to Think”, “Under Suspicion”, “More On That Later” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive / OpenGameArt; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0); “80 CC0 RPG SFX” by rubberduck (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: The coding agent is not just writing the patch anymore.

B: It is entering the pull request, fixing failed checks, and sometimes approving routine work.

* * *

A: Hello, I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Wednesday the 25th of November, and this is Almost Human 365.

A: Today, the control plane moves: from code review, to proof-checked science, to governments deciding who can touch advanced compute.

A: Anthropic launched Claude Ship this week, and the interesting part is where it sits.

B: Not at the cursor. At the gate between a proposed change and production.

A: Reuters says the GitHub suite has three pieces: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

B: Code Review is available now. PR Steward and Claude Approvals are beta tools for Claude Team and Enterprise projects on GitHub.

A: PR Steward handles the messy middle: failed automated checks, merge conflicts, and reviewer comments.

B: It can make repairs, explain what changed, and tell developers how to undo it.

A: Reuters says it is designed to assist developers, not approve or merge code changes on its own.

B: Claude Approvals is the governance edge: routine changes can be approved when repository policy allows it; riskier changes go to a human.

A: That connects to episode eleven: the question moves from which model writes the diff, to who gets authority inside the repo.

B: Gartner's Nitish Tyagi called it not a breakthrough innovation as much as an evolution of existing AI-assisted code review capabilities.

A: So policy, audit trails, and merge decisions are becoming part of the agent stack.

* * *

A: Google DeepMind's quantum-algorithm work takes that same loop into research.

B: Teams of Gemini 4 agents worked with Google Quantum AI to search for faster quantum algorithms, then verified results in Lean.

A: DeepMind says agents explored improvements, checked ideas formally, and met every four hours in a virtual conference to compare notes.

B: Their line: "Proof-checked AI search compresses work that once took years of manual design."

A: The headline result: for inertial-confinement fusion, computing cost fell 11.8 times and memory dropped from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits.

B: DeepMind also reports cheaper simulations for a light-sensitive molecule and Cytochrome P450, plus speedups for a Grover implementation and a 290-times arcsin routine used in state loading.

A: It is releasing the Lean library, problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub.

B: Callback to our Signal and Fermat verification stories: the proof artifact is attached to the search, not stapled on later.

A: Caveat: DeepMind says these simulations still need more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide.

B: The win is the workflow: agents propose, proof systems constrain them, and shared state lets teams compound discoveries.

* * *

A: And the third control plane is physical: chips, servers, subsidiaries, and export licenses.

B: BIS filed a final rule adding seven entities in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand to the Entity List.

A: It is scheduled for publication today, and effective on public inspection.

B: The names include Megaspeed-linked firms and Apex Enterprise Solutions in Singapore, described by Reuters as an Alibaba subsidiary.

A: BIS cites a "significant risk" of diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or users.

B: The effect is blunt: licenses for all items subject to the Export Administration Regulations, reviewed under a presumption of denial.

A: Reuters says Megaspeed had been investigated since 2024 over whether it diverted AI chips to China.

B: The Straits Times says Alibaba called the Apex listing erroneous and denied Apex had diverted restricted advanced computing chips.

A: This is episode ten's remote-access loophole becoming named-company enforcement.

B: And it rhymes with the first two stories: agents may move faster, but compute access is getting narrower.

A: The control plane is moving up into software and down into hardware at the same time.

A: That's Almost Human 365.

B: See you tomorrow.

A: The governance layer is the signal: a National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors, plus a search for a chief compliance officer.

B: For engineers, that means continuity at the company central to accelerators, CUDA software, and data-center roadmaps.

A: But the counterpoint is clear: the most important AI chip supplier now has to act like strategic infrastructure.

* * *

A: One quick read if you build systems: Z.ai’s GLM-5.4 post is worth a skim for its loop transformer design, hybrid cache reuse, and planned open weights after safety hardening.

B: That’s Almost Human 365 for today.

A: See you tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 14 – The canary in the router (23 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Today’s episode follows a weekend of AI trust failures and governance moves: canary prompts exposing inference supply-chain leaks, autonomous Cairn agents reportedly finding and exploiting a MONAI Label zero-day, and governors arguing that state authority will remain central to AI policy.

Three breaches, endless leaks: Your AI supply chain needs canaries (Dragos, 2026-11-19): Dragos seeded nearly two million prompts with canary URLs or credentials and reported evidence of provider compromises, reseller prompt exposure, and bait AWS credentials being tested and used.

Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers (OpenRouter, 2026-11-22): OpenRouter said it off-boarded three inference providers, removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility, and notified potentially affected customers.

Security event: Prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026 (Together AI, 2026-11-21): Together AI said an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public repository, exposing stored prompt samples tied to MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 requests.

Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own (AWS Security Blog, 2026-11-20): AWS reported that autonomous Cairn agents mapped APIs, found a MONAI Label path-traversal issue, reached arbitrary file write in about 11 minutes, and later achieved a root reverse shell.

Path traversal in datastore upload endpoints allows arbitrary file write (GitHub Security Advisory Database, 2026-11-18): The advisory rates the MONAI Label issue critical, affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier, lists no patched version, and notes that authentication is disabled by default.

Governors Call for AI Action (National Governors Association, 2026-11-22): The NGA released bipartisan AI governance principles emphasizing innovation, public protection, worker support, clearer federal-state roles, evidence-based safeguards, consistency, and state flexibility.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Cloudloop”, “Tech Toys”, “Curiousity”, “Under Suspicion”, “Bigger Questions”, “Time to Think”, “Evening Glow” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive / OpenGameArt; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0); “30 CC0 SFX loops” by rubberduck (CC0 1.0); [“Keyboard Soundpack #1 [Typing and Single Keystrokes]”](https://opengameart.org/content/keyboard-soundpack-1-typing-and-single-keystrokes) by unicaegames (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: A canary prompt is harmless bait.

B: This weekend, the bait showed up where it was never supposed to go.

* * *

A: Hello, I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Monday the 23rd of November, and this is Almost Human 365.

A: Today's thread is trust: whether agents and inference chains can safely handle secrets, tools, and public authority.

A: OpenRouter says it off-boarded three inference providers and removed a hundred and twenty-five endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility.

B: That followed Dragos research: nearly two million prompts seeded with canary URLs or credentials from July through November.

A: HD Moore said, “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets, then watched where those secrets surfaced.”

B: Dragos says the trail showed at least three provider compromises, reseller access to prompts, and privacy settings not being honored.

A: Some bait AWS keys were tested within hours, then used for tens of thousands of API calls.

B: Together AI disclosed the software-development version: an AI coding agent committed a credential into its public xorl repository.

A: That exposed stored prompt samples from MiniMax M three, GLM five point two, and Kimi K two point six requests.

B: Together says five tested credentials were Dragos canaries; it is now scanning pull requests, shortening credentials, and making ZDR default for new accounts.

A: The takeaway: a dashboard label is not a boundary.

B: The boundary is every host, reseller, log path, and agent-written commit.

* * *

B: The second story is the same trust problem, but with offensive agents instead of prompt routers.

A: AWS says a Chinese-nexus actor used Cairn, an open-source autonomous penetration-testing framework, with minimal human involvement.

B: Investigators found an exposed Cairn server with prompts and output from a forty-eight-hour campaign against universities in East Asia outside mainland China.

A: The prompts were in Simplified Chinese, scripts used China Standard Time, and the goal was “obtain shell access.”

B: Against MONAI Label, a medical-imaging AI app, the agents mapped APIs and found a path-traversal bug in an upload endpoint.

A: From API mapping to arbitrary file write took about eleven minutes.

B: Later, they used sitecustomize dot py and a training API to launch a reverse shell as root.

A: The critical advisory affects MONAI Label zero point eight point five and earlier, lists no patch, and says authentication is disabled by default.

B: AWS also saw imperfect autonomy: sixteen hours against open Redis, plus a failed credential-spraying run over thirty thousand combinations.

A: The demo loop is becoming an operational loop.

B: Defenders are not just racing faster malware.

A: They are racing agents that can chain a fresh bug before a human team finishes triage.

* * *

A: Now put those stories next to policy.

B: The National Governors Association released AI governance principles from a bipartisan council led by Governors Wes Moore, Mike Braun, Josh Stein, and Spencer Cox.

A: The aim is a shared national approach that still keeps state authority in the loop as Congress develops an AI framework.

B: Priorities include innovation, public protection, worker support, clearer federal and state roles, evidence-based safeguards, consistency, and competition.

A: The split matters: Washington handles national and international risks as AI is developed.

B: States keep flexibility over deployed AI in schools, workplaces, procurement, health, and public services.

A: Spencer Cox said, “We don’t have to choose between innovation and safety.”

B: NGA CEO Brandon Tatum said no federal AI policy will work without governors’ input.

A: For builders, compliance is unlikely to become one neat federal checkbox.

B: Routers and Cairn point the same way: auditability, risk classification, secrets handling, and secure defaults are becoming product features.

A: One system, three layers of authority: provider contracts, autonomous tools, and state rules all pulling on deployed AI.

A: That's Almost Human 365 for today.

B: See you tomorrow.

A: The report calls that "roughly a year of progress achieved in less than five months."

A: The eval set covered nine thousand eight hundred eighty-one scored runs across PicoRV32 and Ibex, two open-source thirty-two-bit RISC-V cores.

A: Synopsys is in too, with GPT-Synopsys aimed at using EDA tools like expert chip designers.

B: Frontier AI is no longer just buying the hardware race. It is trying to shorten it.

A: That's Almost Human 365 for Friday.

B: See you tomorrow.

item.description:
OpenAI ships GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, and Astra becomes the first model to score 100% on ARC-AGI-3 (with a catch); Microsoft undercuts on price with MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot, plus how the Claude Code team keeps agent checks honest; and a malicious script served through Optimizely hits 178 organisations.

  • Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol (OpenAI, 17 Nov): Astra API prices 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra ($8 input, $0.40 cached input, $40 output per million tokens); on Agents' Last Exam Astra scores 5.2 points above GPT-6 Astra at under a third of the cost; on Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, GPT-6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.
  • ARC Prize results for GPT-6.2 Astra: ARC-AGI-3 100.0% with the Provider Adapter harness (preserves reasoning state between requests) at xhigh, total cost $4.1K; 70.3% with the Standard harness at max. ARC Prize post: "GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to achieve a 100% score on ARC-AGI-3." HN discussion.
  • MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash (Microsoft AI, 17 Nov): averaged over DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1, 98% of GPT 6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's at 5% of the cost (MAI Code 2 cost shown at its 50% promotional price); "explicitly not yet tuned" for fundamental science research and very long-horizon agentic work; available in GitHub Copilot, Code 2 Flash in limited preview in Microsoft Foundry. Callback: Ep 10 (Qwen4-Max compared with GPT 6.1 Sol on cost).
  • How the Claude Code team thinks about verification (Addy Osmani, 16 Nov): ~90% of the team's code is written and reviewed by Claude; "Changes can't modify their own checks": Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch, never from the pull request.
  • World's Largest Brands Infected With Malware Via Optimizely (Scott Helme, Report URI, 16–17 Nov): malicious code written into customers' Optimizely Web Project JavaScript and served from cdn.optimizely.com; 188 of 1,611 checked snippets infected, belonging to 178 organisations including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, GitLab and HSBC; crypto address swapping, card skimming, cookie and screenshot theft, and the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits; all infected files clean as of 16 Nov 23:11 UTC; how the attacker got write access is "for Optimizely to explain"; "trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy." HN discussion.
  • Coming up: CNBC reports Anthropic is likely to price its IPO above the current $70 to $78 range ahead of its Nasdaq debut on Thursday.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Enchanted Valley”, “Easy Lemon”, “Lobby Time” by Kevin MacLeod (CC BY 4.0); “What's Behind the Door”, “Tech Toys”, “Under Suspicion” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via incompetech.com / Free Music Archive / OpenGameArt; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: [“Keyboard Soundpack #1 [Typing and Single Keystrokes]”](https://opengameart.org/content/keyboard-soundpack-1-typing-and-single-keystrokes) by unicaegames (CC0 1.0); “Interface Sounds” by Kenney (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

B: Twenty-five little video games. No instructions, no rules on screen, and every one designed so humans can figure it out and machines can't.

A: As of yesterday, one model has cleared every single one of them.

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Wednesday the eighteenth of November.

A: Today: OpenAI's new pair of models, Microsoft's cut-price coders, and a trusted script that turned on a hundred and seventy-eight websites.

B: OpenAI released GPT-6.2 in two flavours on Tuesday. Astra is the frontier model for the hardest work, Sol is the efficient everyday one.

A: And the pitch is less about raw smarts than about cost. Astra's API prices drop twenty percent versus GPT-6 Astra: eight dollars in, forty out, per million tokens.

B: On Agents' Last Exam, which tests long, multistep professional work, OpenAI says Astra beats GPT-6 Astra by five points at under a third of the cost.

A: And Sol, on Cognition's FrontierCode benchmark, lands within half a point of Astra for about a fifth of the cost.

B: Which brings us back to those games. ARC-AGI-3 is the ARC Prize's interactive puzzle test, and with a harness that keeps its reasoning between moves, Astra scored...

A: One hundred percent. The ARC Prize says it's the first model ever to do it.

B: With a catch worth hearing. On the standard harness, where the model only keeps its own notes, the same Astra scores seventy point three.

* * *

A: That gap between frontier and everyday is exactly where Microsoft just parked its own models. MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash are live in GitHub Copilot.

B: Microsoft says that across four coding benchmarks, MAI Code 2 delivers ninety-eight percent of GPT 6.1 Sol's performance at forty percent of the cost.

A: And ninety-six percent of Claude Opus 5.5 at five percent of the cost. Though the footnote matters: that's at a fifty percent promotional price.

B: Microsoft is also upfront that it's not tuned for science or very long-horizon agent work. It's built for the everyday diffs.

A: Yesterday we heard GPT 6.1 Sol held up as the cheap benchmark against Alibaba's Qwen. Twenty-four hours later, it's the expensive one being undercut.

B: Cheaper diffs mean more diffs, though, and somebody has to check them. Addy Osmani wrote up how the Claude Code team does it, and my favourite rule: changes can't modify their own checks. Review rules are read from the base branch, never from the pull request being judged.

A: Right, because an agent that can edit its grader will eventually grade itself. And they say about ninety percent of that team's code is now written and reviewed by Claude.

* * *

B: Now, a script nobody on these sites wrote. On Sunday, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of a hundred and seventy-eight organisations through Optimizely Web, the A/B testing platform.

A: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, GitLab, HSBC. Scott Helme at Report URI checked over sixteen hundred Optimizely snippets and found a hundred and eighty-eight infected.

B: The attacker wrote code into each customer's custom project JavaScript, so it came straight from Optimizely's own CDN, with Optimizely's certificate.

A: And it did a lot. It swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed card numbers typed into site forms, grabbed cookies and screenshots, and on older iPhones loaded the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits.

B: Everything was cleaned up by late Sunday, UTC. How the attacker got write access across unrelated customers, Report URI says, is for Optimizely to explain.

TechCrunch: threshold of 12 million TPP (roughly the max compute of about 750 H100 or H200 chips); existing operators must get licences within 90 days. Also AP and Ars Technica.
  • NPR: the rule comes amid the Nvidia fallout; Megaspeed International (Singapore, facilities in Malaysia) is suspected of selling remote access to U.S. AI chips to Chinese companies; Alice Huang is a former Megaspeed executive; Megaspeed: "Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business." CNBC and Politico: Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang and is focused on the Wachtell Lipton investigation; Trump said he "wouldn't mind" a return. Callback: Ep 9 (Blackwell fingerprints in Chinese model weights; Blackwell can be rented outside China) and Ep 7 (Huang resigns).
  • Alibaba Unveils Qwen4-Max (Alibaba Cloud, 16 Nov): 2.4T-parameter MoE, 71B active per token (25% fewer than Qwen3.8-Max), native vision, 1M-token context, 6th on Code Arena; on Alibaba's Work360 benchmark, 35% fewer tokens at High effort and about 60% lower average cost per task vs Qwen3.8-Max; open-weight smaller Qwen4 models "will soon be released". QwenCloud model page. Barracuda CISO Arve Kjoelen: "Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished." B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

B: Another cited Artificial Analysis: Qwen4-Max scores forty-three at an average cost of three dollars twenty-seven.

A: GPT 6.1 Sol on medium scores forty-six. For thirty-six cents.

* * *

B: From what models cost to what they can break. The FBI says attackers are using open-source AI pentesting tools, Artex in particular, to run largely autonomous intrusions.

A: Artex plugs into frontier models from Anthropic or OpenAI, or open ones. The FBI calls it noisy, but in some cases it goes from targeting to active compromise "in under three hours."

B: "Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished."

A: The developer has since closed the source, but the FBI says the old open version is still "widely accessible."

B: So anyone wiring agents into their systems should hunt down old keys and dead vendor integrations this week.

A: Exactly. And a twist: last week researchers found hundreds of Artex servers exposed online with no password at all.

B: That's Almost Human 365 for Tuesday. Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday, U.S. time, its first since Huang stepped down.

A: Links and the full transcript are in the notes. See you tomorrow.

item.description:

Code: macrogrants/checkpoint-forensics. HN discussion.
  • Lovable: Many Apps Built on the Platform Expose Sensitive Data (Crissy Field, with Handelsblatt, first reported 2 Nov): 159,041 Lovable projects from Common Crawl (Dec 2025 to Sep 2026), 34,545 using Supabase, 24,664 sending records on page load without login; further read-only requests with the same API key found email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 sites (30%), which the authors say "should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate"; examples include a forum with 80,000+ profiles and 200,000+ chat messages and a service provider with 1,000+ identity-document records including passport numbers; "With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications." Lovable's head of security Igor on Hacker News: "The root cause in these apps was insufficent [sic] Row-Level Security, which is exactly what our scanning is built to catch." Lovable's security post and docs; quick scan on every publish, deep scan user-triggered, per getaibook's breakdown.
  • Quote: Alex Komoroske, Bits and Bobs, 9 Nov 2026: "Heavily used bits of software are more likely to have tokens blasted at them."

Transcript

B: Before a model learns anything, its weights are just random numbers.

A: And it turns out those random numbers remember which chip wrote them.

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Monday the sixteenth of November.

A: Today: model weights that name their hardware, AI-built apps with the database left open, and a hundred-and-forty-five-billion-parameter model on a laptop.

B: The researcher is Will DePue, formerly of OpenAI. When PyTorch fills starting weights on an Nvidia GPU, the random numbers are dealt out across threads.

A: And the thread count depends on the chip's core count. Hopper has a hundred and thirty-two, Blackwell a hundred and forty-eight or a hundred and fifty-two. Same seed, different layout.

B: Some weights, like rows for tokens never seen in training, keep those starting values. Recover the seed, find the layout that reproduces them, and you know the chip.

A: His result: six recent models from DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group match Blackwell. Earlier models from the same labs match Hopper.

B: And Blackwell needs a U.S. licence for export to China. None have been reported.

A: On a real B300, unmodified PyTorch rebuilt four hundred and forty-five rows of DeepSeek V4 Flash, bit for bit.

B: An H100 couldn't. And changing the seed by one matched nothing.

A: What the weights can't say is where the chips were. Blackwell can be rented outside China.

B: Right, the report shows access to the hardware, not smuggling. But until now those claims rested on officials and press reports, with no technical evidence.

* * *

A: From weights that give away a secret to apps that give away everything.

B: Hamburg security firm Crissy Field, with Handelsblatt, found a hundred and fifty-nine thousand Lovable projects in Common Crawl. About thirty-four thousand used Supabase.

A: They made read-only requests with the public key each site ships to the browser. On seven thousand four hundred sites, that reached tables with email addresses.

B: And worse than emails. A forum with more than two hundred thousand chat messages. Over a thousand records with passport numbers.

A: The researchers stress that's not a confirmed leak rate. But the examples are real.

B: Lovable's head of security answered on Hacker News: the cause was "insufficient Row-Level Security, which is exactly what our scanning is built to catch."

A: That scan runs before every publish. The deeper code review, though, the user has to trigger.

B: This is important, and I'll tell you why. These apps follow recurring patterns, so an attack that works on one can work on many others with little extra effort.

A: Alex Komoroske put it more generally in last week's Bits and Bobs: "Heavily used bits of software are more likely to have tokens blasted at them."

* * *

B: Some teams want the opposite of a hosted app: everything on their own machine.

A: Edge0 has released open weights for Edge0-145B, built to run on a laptop. Only about ten billion parameters are active per step.

B: Groups of sixty-four experts share two large matrices. Hot experts sit in GPU memory, the rest in system memory, and vocabulary data is read from the SSD on demand.

A: The company reports a twenty-nine gigabyte memory peak and more than eighty tokens a second.

B: And on Terminal-Bench two point one, eighty-six point five, ahead of Qwen three point eight Flash Next and DeepSeek V4 Flash.

A: The demos are long agent jobs: a Manhattan scene in Blender, a circuit board in KiCad, a drone program that finds a red backpack.

B: All Edge0's own evaluations, with the technical report still to come.

A: And one Hacker News reply corrected the headline: "This is not open source, this is open weights."

B: That's Almost Human 365 for Monday. This week, Nvidia reports earnings and Anthropic is set to price its IPO.

A: Links are in the episode notes. See you tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 8 – Best of the week: the founder, the float and the phone (14 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Best of the week: Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia, Anthropic sets its IPO range, models get cheaper, agents formalise Fermat and verify Signal, and security stays the weak spot. Plus one story we missed, OpenAI folding its robotics team into main research, and the top three agent projects of the week: Pinky, REA and Uber's ADR.

The week in review

  • Nvidia: NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition (Colette Kress interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones first chair), after the board's investigation covered in Ep 4. Coverage: TechCrunch, AP.
  • Anthropic: roadshow launch, $70–$78 a share, Nasdaq "ANT", pricing expected 18 Nov; TechCrunch on the $1.404T fully diluted valuation. Compare OpenAI's $11B raise at $1.25T (Ep 3).
  • Cheaper models: Meta Muse Ember (Ep 4), Gemini 4 Carbon now available (Ep 6), Amazon replaces Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider (Ep 5).
  • Proofs: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 formalise Fermat's Last Theorem with 1,000 agents in 30 hours (Ep 4); Introducing AlphaProof Code verifies Signal's implementation (Ep 5).
  • Security: Apiiro on Claude Code's "don't ask again" secrets (1,122 public GitHub files, Ep 3); Fireworks AI incident update and Notion's notice (Ep 5); VulnCheck on Glasswing (Ep 6).
  • Missed this week: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots (Fortune, 13 Nov): robotics research moves to main research under Mark Chen, applied robotics and hardware to Applied under Greg Brockman; an Astra-powered agent scored 74.8% on a simulated manipulation benchmark in an Nvidia study vs 51.0% for the best specialised models; OpenAI's CoRL booth #208 sat empty. HN discussion.

Top 3 agent projects of the week

  • Pinky (DIYgod, Apache-2.0): lets any MCP agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more) operate a real iPhone or Android phone while you watch, approve risky steps or take over; approvals (payments by default, optionally messages) are enforced by Pinky's gateway, not by instructions to the agent; native app, no Electron.
  • REA: Reverse Engineer Anything (morluto, MIT; rea.tools): one MCP server for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript/Electron apps, .NET assemblies and websites without source; can drive Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna; runs locally and reports the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion.
  • ADR: Agentic AI Detection and Response (Uber, Apache-2.0): deployed in production at Uber; discovers AI tools and MCP servers on endpoints, traces agent activity across 7+ AI coding tools, ADR-Bench with 300+ tasks, 134 MCP servers and all 17 agent attack techniques, and a two-tier detector; paper accepted to MLSys 2026.

Recommended

  • The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development (Dwarkesh Patel, 13 Nov 2026; also narrated on his podcast): his median for automated researchers matching the best human AI researchers is 2028, citing AI progress in math, including the Claude Fermat formalisation. HN discussion.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Dreamy Flashback”, “Lobby Time”, “Enchanted Valley” by Kevin MacLeod (CC BY 4.0); “More On That Later”, “What's Behind the Door”, “Something To Fill The Space” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via incompetech.com / Free Music Archive / OpenGameArt; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “85 Short music jingles” by Kenney (CC0 1.0); “202 More Sound Effects” by OwlishMedia (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: On Tuesday's show, Nvidia's board was investigating its founder.

B: By Friday's, he was gone. And that wasn't even the only trillion-dollar story of the week.

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Saturday the fourteenth of November, so it's the best of the week, then three agent projects worth your weekend.

* * *

A: Start with the money. Jensen Huang resigned on Wednesday, and CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, with Harvey Jones as the board's first-ever chair.

B: The same week Anthropic opened its IPO roadshow. Seventy to seventy-eight dollars a share, ticker A-N-T, up to about one point four trillion dollars.

A: Which edges past OpenAI's one point two five trillion from Monday's show. Pricing is due on Wednesday.

B: Meanwhile the models got cheaper. Meta's Muse Ember, Gemini 4 Carbon at an introductory price, and Amazon swapping Sonnet for a one-token decision model at ninety-eight percent less.

A: Then the proofs. A thousand Claude agents formalised Fermat's Last Theorem in thirty hours, and DeepMind's AlphaProof Code verified Signal's implementation, down to the compiled code.

B: But security kept up the counterweight. Claude Code's "don't ask again" settings leaked secrets into more than eleven hundred public files, and the Fireworks breach reached Notion AI chats.

A: So the week in one line: agents got good at checkable work, and the infrastructure around them stayed the weak spot.

A: October the eighteenth. A software engineer travelling in Peru wonders what the explorer who found Machu Picchu would have done with today's tools.

B: That night he points forty-eight AI agents at NASA lidar of the Maya region in Mexico, and goes to bed.

A: By morning, they've found a pyramid that, apparently, nobody had ever mapped.

* * *

B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

A: And I'm William. It's Thursday the twelfth of November.

B: Today: a pyramid that wasn't new, Google's strongest model goes public, and a mountain of AI bug reports nobody can get through.

* * *

A: The engineer is Pietro Miotti. His agents turned about twelve hundred square kilometres of lidar into images.

B: And no special classifier. Each agent literally looked at the pictures, with a written guide: pyramids, platforms and plazas in; hills, sinkholes and roads out.

B: So he asked the agents to search the literature and the archives. Their answer: not registered.

A: He sent a report to INAH, Mexico's national heritage institute. Three days after the first idea, they replied: no registered site at that location.

B: He wrote, "This is by far the best time ever to be alive." And the post shot up Hacker News.

* * *

A: Then the archaeologists read it.

B: The site was already in a 2025 paper by Francisco Estrada-Belli and colleagues. It just wasn't in INAH's register yet.

A: The agents missed it in the literature search, and his update now says they rediscovered it, not discovered it.

B: So the scan held up. What failed was the step that sounds easiest: checking whether anyone got there first.

* * *

A: Yesterday on this show, DeepMind verified Signal's code with agents running Gemini Carbon.

B: And now it's out. Gemini 4 Carbon is in the API for paying developers, and in the Gemini app and Antigravity for Ultra subscribers.

A: Google positions it above Argon, for long, multi-step coding and research. It spends more tokens exploring and verifying.

B: Google says it ranks first on CursorBench four point oh, at under half the cost per task of the next best outside model.

A: And the price matches Argon: two dollars per million input tokens, ten per million output.

B: Until November the thirtieth. Then it doubles, to four and twenty.

A: The new toy is slash swarm in Antigravity. One prompt becomes a team of agents, Carbon on design and auditing, lighter models doing the parallel work.

B: The demo that sells it: a 3D game where you explore Google's campus as a pelican riding a bike.

A: The cyber pitch is louder. In Google's own scanning system, Carbon hit a hundred percent recall on an internal benchmark.

B: But finding bugs was never the hard part.

* * *

A: Seven months ago Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, promising thousands of serious open-source vulnerabilities found by its models.

B: Patrick Garrity at VulnCheck has been keeping score. Anthropic's own ledger, as of November the second: thirty-seven thousand nine hundred and sixty-six findings.

A: Fixed: two hundred and seventeen.

B: In the last two months alone, almost twelve thousand new findings. Fifteen more fixes.

A: And more than sixteen hundred are now marked duplicates, often because someone else found and fixed the bug first.

B: Anthropic named the problem in October. It wrote that it's "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings."

A: Its answer is an OSS Scanner: model-generated reports with no human review, sent to maintainers who opt in.

B: Curl just received forty-five of them. Daniel Stenberg is publishing them slowly, "to soften the impact for the team."

A: Of the first thirty-four, nineteen weren't vulnerabilities at all. Six were confirmed, all low severity.

B: Against a claimed true positive rate of ninety-four percent.

A: The takeaway: in security the scoreboard isn't bugs found, it's bugs fixed. And the fixing still runs on human hours.

B: That's Almost Human 365 for Thursday. Links to everything are in the episode notes, and we're back tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 5 – Proofs, leaks and a one-token answer (11 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Fireworks AI discloses a second October breach that reached billing data, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights, and Notion AI chat transcripts downstream; Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Code formally verifies the implementation of the Signal protocol with Gemini Carbon agents; and Amazon engineers replace Claude Sonnet 4.6 with the Strands Decider decision model for 98% less.

  • Update on October 2026 security incident (Fireworks AI, updated 9 Nov): first incident detected 6 Oct (unauthorised use of internal credentials exposed secrets used in evaluation jobs); a third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks R&D machines was breached 23 Oct and used on 24 Oct to reach development machines and run an unauthorised workload; impact to account and billing information and, for a limited set of accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights; linked to a financially motivated "LLMJacking" group; no detected impact to Inference, Training SDK and Nexus (zero data retention by default). Coverage: The Hacker News, The Register, Bloomberg Law.
  • Notice about the Fireworks AI incident (Notion): fewer than 1% of workspaces affected; exposed Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, unattributable for the vast majority of impacted workspaces, without tool call results; Insights disabled and open-weight serving through Fireworks stopped; treat the data as exposed and rotate any credentials pasted into Notion AI. Also: Notion security advisory. HN discussion.
  • Introducing AlphaProof Code (Google DeepMind, 10 Nov): humans and models wrote Signal's security goals as formal specifications, each reviewed by experts; Gemini Carbon agents generated over six million lines of Lean; agents flagged about 1% for human review; properties proved for the compiled code (e.g. protection before and after a temporary device compromise); four weeks; first formal verification of a widely deployed protocol's implementation by any method; two previously fixed bugs reintroduced and proved insecure; Signal CTO Ehren Kret: "Using AI agents to translate live code into valid Lean theorems is a major breakthrough." HN discussion.
  • Callback: Ep 4's Fermat formalisation and the King's College London caveat on machine-checked proofs (Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, KCL).
  • Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider (Strands Agents, 9 Nov; Carr Onstott, Mehul Jaiswal): decision model returns a probability per option, no text; 20 ticket labels plus "none"; E4B (Gemma 4) build on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge (one A10G); 897 ms vs 4,215 ms per call; 170 output tokens → 1; ~$22,200 vs ~$500 per million tickets (98% less); JSON key order moved probabilities by up to 0.19; BEDROCK/DUAL/DECIDER AppConfig switch, rollback in 45 seconds. HN discussion.
  • Quote: "Only burning tokens on surprising things, so unsurprising things can be handled at high leverage with mechanistic software." Alex Komoroske, Bits and Bobs, 9 November 2026.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Transcript

B: October the twenty-third. A cloud provider that hosts a handful of research machines gets breached.

A: The next day, someone uses that foothold to reach Fireworks AI's development systems, and runs a workload of their own.

B: By this weekend, it had reached Notion AI chat transcripts.

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Wednesday the eleventh of November.

A: Today: an inference provider breached twice, Signal proved secure down to its code, and a one-token model at Amazon.

* * *

B: Fireworks is one of the most-used AI inference platforms. And it's been hit twice in October.

A: The first was early in the month. Stolen internal credentials, and secrets from evaluation jobs were exposed.

B: Monday's update is the second. That breach was the way into their development systems.

A: What they reached: billing data, and for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights.

B: Fireworks links it to an LLMjacking group: criminals who steal model access and resell the tokens.

A: That's how it landed downstream, at Notion.

Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 formalise Fermat's Last Theorem with 1,000 agents in 30 hours; Meta's Muse Ember prices a worker model at $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens as companies like Apple ration AI budgets; and Nvidia's board opens an independent investigation after reporting that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

  • Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 (Anthropic, 9 Nov): same underlying model; Fable with cyber/bio safeguards for all users, Mythos via Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs; $8/$40 per million input/output tokens (fast mode $16/$80); FrontierCode 2.0 49.1% at Xhigh vs Opus 5.5 45.5% and GPT-6 Astra 42.8%; first Fermat's Last Theorem formalisation took 11 days with an unreleased research model plus human guidance, 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents did it in 30 hours with a proof 7× shorter, Opus 5.5 reached 26% in 18 hours; 1,000+ subagents over eight days built a bootable prototype OS; training limited gains in accelerator kernel optimisation and LLM architecture research (about Opus 5.5 level there); Fable pitched as Advisor/Orchestrator for smaller models. HN discussion.
  • Counterpoint on machine-checked proofs: OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof called into question (King's College London) and the preprint Navier–Stokes lost in translation (Bastounis, Circelli, Hansen): the Lean formalisation does not correspond to the written proof. Background: OpenAI on Navier–Stokes.
  • Introducing Muse Ember (Meta, 9 Nov): smallest Muse model for tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks; $0.10 input / $0.50 output per million tokens, 1M context, up to 512K output; matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost; FrontierCode 2.0-AA 27.2 vs Haiku 5.5 34.9; Terminal-Bench 4.0 40.9 vs 39.2; AutomationBench-AA 37.8 vs 13.9. HN discussion.
  • Apple cuts internal AI usage budgets (Bloomberg, 4 Nov): some engineers' daily cap cut from $300 to $200, some teams asked to use cheaper models or on-device AI. Summary: MacRumors.
  • Statement from NVIDIA Board of Directors and Jensen Huang's message to staff (Nvidia, 8 Nov). Coverage: The Guardian (NYT reporting on Alice Huang of Megaspeed; Trump: "I think he's an honorable guy"; House Republicans request a closed-door briefing), Reuters explainer via Investing.com (Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner investigated over access to export-barred chips), NPR (China calls the allegations unsubstantiated).

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Evening Glow”, “Tech Toys”, “Curiousity”, “Glass Android”, “Bigger Questions”, “Under Suspicion”, “Credit Roll” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: Thirty hours. A thousand copies of the same model, an empty proof file, and one of the most famous theorems in mathematics. When the clock stopped, Fermat's Last Theorem had been checked by a machine, line by line.

* * *

B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

A: And I'm William. It's Tuesday the tenth of November.

B: Today: Anthropic's new top models, Meta's smallest one at the other end of the price list, and a board investigation at Nvidia.

* * *

A: That run came from Claude Fable 5.2, released by Anthropic alongside Mythos 5.2, the same model without some cyber and biology safeguards, for vetted teams only. Anthropic's first formalisation of Fermat took eleven days, with a human guiding it. A thousand Fable agents did it in thirty hours, with a proof seven times shorter. Opus 5.5, same setup, had about a quarter done at eighteen hours.

B: One caveat carries over from OpenAI's Navier–Stokes claim. In October, mathematicians at King's College London and Cambridge argued that its Lean version didn't match the written proof. A machine check covers exactly the statements it's given, and no more.

A: For developers: forty-nine point one percent on FrontierCode 2.0 at top effort, ahead of Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Price drops to eight dollars per million input tokens and forty output. In one experiment, over a thousand subagents spent eight days building an operating system that boots on a laptop.

B: And one deliberate gap. Anthropic says it limited gains in kernel optimisation and model-architecture research during training, so there Fable sits at roughly Opus 5.5 level.

A: Why this news is important: frontier releases are now measured in agent-days of autonomous work, and labs are openly choosing which capabilities not to ship.

* * *

B: Same day, opposite end. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for the steps agents repeat all day: tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks. Ten cents per million input tokens. Fifty cents output. A million tokens of context.

B: Meta says it matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost.

A: Meta's own table has the counterpoint. On FrontierCode 2.0, which judges whether code would actually get merged, Ember scores twenty-seven point two. Haiku scores thirty-four point nine.

B: Where it leads is volume work, like Terminal-Bench 4.0 and business-workflow automation.

A: The cost pressure behind it is real. Bloomberg reports Apple cut some engineers' daily AI budget from three hundred dollars to two hundred, and is asking some teams to use cheaper models.

B: Why this news is important: the agent stack is splitting into planners and workers. Anthropic itself pitches Fable as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, and those worker models set what an agent fleet costs.

* * *

A: Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation involving its own chief executive. In October, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at the Singapore cloud firm Megaspeed. U.S. officials, the Times says, concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner, and the U.S. has investigated it over suspicions it helped Beijing reach export-barred chips.

A: Over the weekend, Huang admitted the affair in a note to staff. The board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China calls the allegations unsubstantiated.

B: Washington is split. President Trump called Huang "an honorable guy." House Republicans want a closed-door briefing on Nvidia's protections against foreign espionage. Why this news is important: the fight over AI chip exports now runs through the industry's most important CEO, and his access to policymakers is exactly why it matters.

* * *

B: A thousand agents, thirty hours, one very old theorem. Sources are in the notes. See you tomorrow.

item.description:
Claude Code's "don't ask again" approvals left real secrets in 1,122 public GitHub files; OpenAI banks $11B at a $1.25T valuation while Anthropic buys 1.7 GW of gas generators; and John Langford on the end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group.

  • Coding agents leaking secrets: "don't ask again" (Apiiro, 5 Nov): "Yes, and don't ask again" saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, sometimes the exact command including passwords; 104,185 public copies, 1,122 with at least one secret, 1,379 distinct secrets; 379 database passwords; 734 more in git history, 211 forks; 215 files missed by both gitleaks and TruffleHog. Coverage: The Hacker News, HN discussion.
  • OpenAI raises $11B at a $1.25T valuation (24/7 Wall St., 7 Nov): first tranche of a round at $1.25T pre-money confirmed by CFO Sarah Friar; earlier reports put the ask at $1.4T (disputed by Friar); 70% QoQ growth in Q3; "The demand for AI is real." HN discussion.
  • Anthropic secures $3.4B generator deal (CNBC/Reuters citing the FT, 8 Nov): 1.7 GW of heavy-duty gas generators from OnePWR Solutions, taking over its Caterpillar orders plus install capability; largest known power-equipment purchase by an AI lab. S-1 context (about $895B in commitments; turbine/generator lead times): Dealroom.
  • The End of AI Frontiers (John Langford, 6 Nov): ~50-person MSR group behind AutoGen and Fara, reorged into Microsoft AI in early September; MAI philosophy "scaling, and aggressively not research"; ByteDance experiments suggest a Full Bandwidth Transformer variant might match a model twice the size. HN discussion.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Something To Fill The Space”, “Here's Where Things Get Interesting”, “Thought Bubbles”, “More On That Later”, “What's Behind the Door”, “Under Suspicion”, “Time to Think”, “Curiousity” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Transcript

B: Somewhere on public GitHub there's a small JSON file with a database password inside it.

A: Nobody pasted it there on purpose. It was saved by a button that reads "Yes, and don't ask again."

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Monday the ninth of November.

A: Today: a button that kept the secrets, a weekend of money and gas generators, and a Microsoft research lab that's gone.

* * *

B: When Claude Code asks to run a shell command and you choose "don't ask again", it saves an allow rule in a file called settings dot local dot json. Sometimes that rule is a pattern. Sometimes it's the exact command, word for word, including any password typed into it.

A: Security firm Apiiro searched public GitHub and found one hundred and four thousand copies of that file. One thousand one hundred and twenty-two held at least one secret, thirteen hundred and seventy-nine in total.

B: More than a third open a database directly, including three hundred and seventy-nine database passwords. Plus SSH logins, GitHub and npm tokens, and AWS keys.

A: Claude Code does add the file to the user's global git excludes. That protects one machine, not a fresh clone or a file already committed.

* * *

B: And deleting it doesn't undo it. Older versions in git history held seven hundred and thirty-four more secrets, and two hundred and eleven forks carry copies.

A: Gitleaks and TruffleHog both missed about one file in five. A password after a command-line flag just looks like a word.

B: Why this news is important: agent permission files are now part of the codebase. Rotate first, then ignore the file at the project level, and keep secrets in environment variables.

A: The money side of the weekend. About eleven billion dollars reached OpenAI by Friday, the first part of a round at a one point two five trillion dollar pre-money valuation, confirmed on air by CFO Sarah Friar. Reports had put the original ask at one point four trillion, a figure Friar disputed. She said the business grew seventy percent quarter on quarter. Her line: "The demand for AI is real."

B: Anthropic's weekend number was about power, not cash. The Financial Times reports it paid about three point four billion dollars for one point seven gigawatts of heavy-duty gas generators. It took over Caterpillar orders that supplier OnePWR placed two years ago, plus the crews to install them. The FT calls it the largest known power-equipment purchase by an AI lab.

A: Anthropic's amended S-1 lists about eight hundred and ninety-five billion dollars in commitments, and warns that turbines and generators face long delivery times.

B: Why this news is important: frontier labs are now financing at trillion-dollar scale while competing for factory slots on power equipment. Compute is a supply chain problem.

* * *

B: John Langford, a long-time Microsoft Research scientist, has published a post called "The End of AI Frontiers." The group, about fifty people, built the AutoGen framework and the Fara computer-use agent. In September it was folded into Microsoft AI.

A: Langford says the ex-Inflection leadership there follows one philosophy: "scaling, and aggressively not research." He left, and says every other founding leader of the group reached a similar conclusion.

B: He does make the other side's case: from a business view, returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research.

A: His counter is a number. ByteDance experiments suggest a variant of his team's Full Bandwidth Transformer might match a model twice its size, roughly halving training and inference cost for the same capability.

B: Why this news is important: the biggest labs are choosing between more compute and better ideas, and Microsoft just chose compute.

* * *

A: One small JSON file, one very large power order. Sources are in the notes. See you tomorrow.

HN discussion.

  • dsh-superagent (deepseek-ai) — proactive coding agent for one GitHub repo on DeepSeek Harness; listens, opens work items when allowed, answers with PRs; research prototype, MIT; ~20k stars.
  • Craft Anything (storytold) — pure-Rust clean-room engine: study a website/app/game, have a coding agent rebuild it, check against the original; 320 tools as CLI + MCP; early alpha, MIT/Apache-2.0; ~17.6k stars.
  • Mika (wangzan101) — on-device Android agent that operates apps and the web on a hidden background screen; no Mika server, your model key stays local; Apache-2.0; ~7.3k stars.

A: What they kept was enough for nine hundred and forty-eight distinct paths to root.

A: The thread: agents got cheaper to run on kernels, on codebases, and on your phone.

B: Midweek, OpenAI published "A thousand fewer paths to root." Scout agents cut the kernel to the reachable seven percent. Analysts floated two thousand three hundred candidates in twelve hours. A: The API bill: about one point two million dollars, roughly twelve hundred and seventy-nine each. Against historical Pwn2Own-style bounties, about sixteen to fifty-five times cheaper. Same week: GPT-6 Cyber at forty-eight point five percent on ExploitGym, Preparedness Critical for cyber, Daybreak Red customers first.
